sourceCapabilities.capturedGarmentSurface: `GarmentSurface` displays one actual captured owned garment below Home’s rail when an installed reconstruction is available. Its 230-high native GL view preserves original geometry/texture, supports drag inspection and offers comparison/recovery. Rendering is limited to focused foreground use. The surface remains separate from the character and explicitly not fitted; room hangers and character outfit meshes remain category previews. Native texture appearance and hardware resource use remain unverified.
sourceCapabilities.liveFaceSource: The local `modules/thread-face-scanner` Expo module and `LiveFaceScreen` use ARKit face mesh, head pose and expression measurements with capture gates and anchor-continuity checks. The capability-gated button requires an installed iOS build and supported TrueDepth hardware; Expo Go, Android and unsupported hardware retain guided RGB capture. Eight checked poses produce averaged SDK face-surface positions with one neutral-front photograph projected as texture. This is an estimated static face surface, not a complete head, measured back/ears/hair, personal body or facial rig.
sourceCapabilities.candidateReviewAndOwnership: Private photograph/3D candidate review precedes explicit activation; failure preserves the previous character. Candidate files use private cache and are pruned on cleanup, startup and local erasure. Photo-face archives retain their own models independently of the selected face: download/open does not activate them; Use this face performs explicit integrity-checked activation, and capture ownership is retained for deletion.
sourceCapabilities.nativeAcceptanceLimits: This source has not been Swift-compiled on Windows. Native module registration, physical pose directions, projection/UV orientation, side texture, facial likeness, permissions, lifecycle, storage/privacy, gestures and performance require an installed build and phone proof. No live scan has been established to work on a phone. See `docs/live-face-native-acceptance.md` and `docs/dressing-room-progress.md`; the original scope remains unfinished.

narrative.overview:
Thread places a chosen character and owned clothing within an authored native 3D room. Warm plaster and oak provide the setting; restrained moss tint identifies actions and selection. Photographs and garment colors supply personal variation. Thread remains a working name.

This is a source milestone for React Native / Expo iOS and Android phones, with native stacks, three bottom tabs and focused tasks. It records implemented rules rather than visual approval. Tablet layouts are outside the product target; existing wardrobe storage, backup/sync and reconstruction privacy remain infrastructure.
keyCharacteristics: Warm light and dark UI roles, separate from lit 3D materials.
Character and room views paired with real wardrobe data and photo rails.
Concise Profile settings and disclosed secondary outfit tools.
Explicit distinction between custom avatars, reconstructed heads and clothing previews.

rules.name: The Semantic Pair Rule
rules.body: Resolve foreground and background together from the active theme; primary and on-primary change together in dark mode.

rules.name: The Material Boundary Rule
rules.body: UI colors identify controls; room material colors describe lit geometry. A shared hex does not make these roles interchangeable.

rules.name: The Preview Truth Rule
rules.body: Keep category shapes, saved photo references, reconstructed surfaces and wearable garments distinct. Room decoration is not the owned inventory.

dos: Do resolve interface colors through useTheme in both appearances.
Do retain native navigation, accessible control names and system text scaling.
Do preserve clothing photo aspect ratios and provenance labels.
Do distinguish saved looks from wear history.
Do retain category buttons and the inventory alternative alongside 3D targeting.
donts: Don't portray category meshes or a standard preview body as measured fit.
Don't treat an image reference or a valid head GLB as a complete character.
Don't use browser asset previews or source checks as native visual-review evidence.
